To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the neural coding of priors and their influence over the intention inference depends on the abstractness of intentions.
the neural mechanisms of hierarchical intention inference are based on the interplay of sensory and prior information and are modulated by abstractness of intentions.
the neural correlates of prior expectations are modulated by both the type of intention (social vs. non-social, superordinate vs. basic), and the relative weight of priors and sensory evidence.
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding the mechanisms of intention inference, a key component of social cognition, and with investigating the neural basis of hierarchical inference in general, a topic that has been largely unexplored so far.
the neural basis of social cognition and the ability to infer other peoples' intentions.
the neural coding of prior expectations during hierarchical intention inference.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mPFC is a key region for hierarchical intention inference and the TPJ plays a key role in integrating prior and sensory evidence in intention inference.
the mPFC, in cooperation with the TPJ, is a key node in the network of brain areas involved in hierarchical intention inference.
the mPFC-TPJ network is involved in the integration of prior and sensory information in the process of intention inference.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the mPFC modulates the relative weight of priors and sensory evidence by adjusting the strength of the backward connectivity from mPFC to TPJ, and this modulation increases as the intention to infer is more abstract (Superordinate and Social).
the fronto-pariateal network is involved in the hierarchical intention inference and the relative weight of the prior and sensory evidence.
the fronto-pariental network is crucial to adjust the interplay between sensory and priors evidence to infer hierarchical intentions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain is able to adjust the interplay between prior expectations and sensory evidence depending on the type of information to infer.
the brain can adjust the balance between prior and sensory evidence in order to infer intentions of different levels of abstraction.
the fronto-pariental network plays a critical role in the adjustment of the relative weight of priors and sensory evidence during intention inference.
